beats.say: On a trip your devices face more risk than at home: unknown networks, unknown hands and moments of rush.
Before you leave, remove work data you will not need. If possible, use a separate travel device from your organisation.
Hotel and conference network names are easy to fake. For work, always switch on your organisation's secure connection, the VPN.
Avoid public USB charging ports at the airport. Use your own adapter in a wall socket, or your own power bank.
When you are back, have support check the device, and change the passwords of accounts you used on the trip.

question.prompt: At the border your laptop was taken away for a while. What now?

options.label: Nothing, they gave it back
options.feedback: If the device was out of your sight, you cannot know what was done to it.

options.label: I stay out of work accounts and tell the security team
options.feedback: Correct. Do not use it for work until a specialist has checked it.

options.label: I reset the device myself
options.feedback: A reset wipes the evidence. Let a specialist decide.

scenes.explain: A device that left your sight can no longer be trusted. That is why you travel with as little data as possible.

spots.label: Evil twin
spots.explain: It copies the real hotel network name but has no password. Attackers set up twins like this.

spots.label: Free lobby network
spots.explain: Having the hotel name in it proves nothing. Ask at reception for the exact name.

spots.label: Open conference network
spots.explain: Traffic on an open network is not encrypted. If you must connect, share your phone's mobile data instead.

scenes.prompt: On the road: safe or a trap?

caption.text: Scan to download the forum materials

cards.explain: An .apk file installs an app on your phone. You do not need an app for slides, check the official site.

body.text: Check-in is after 14:00. Payment is made at reception.

cards.explain: The hotel's own domain, no link, no payment request. A normal confirmation.

body.text: Confirm your card details within 2 hours:

cards.explain: A different domain and an urgent payment demand. Call the hotel yourself to check the booking.

messages.text: Welcome! Breakfast is 07:00 to 10:30 on the ground floor.

cards.explain: No link and no request, just information.

body.text: Dear delegate, to finish registration, send a photo of your passport and your room number here.

cards.explain: Passports are collected on the official registration page, not in an anonymous chat. A room number reveals where you are.

nodes.text: Your talk was great! Could you copy the slides to this flash drive?
nodes.speaker: Attendee (coffee break)
nodes.spoken: Your talk was great! <breath> Could you copy the slides to this flash drive?

choices.label: I politely decline and offer to send them officially
choices.feedback: Good choice. The stranger's drive never touches your laptop.

choices.label: I plug the drive into my laptop
choices.feedback: A stranger's drive can carry malware. Your laptop and work data are now at risk.

nodes.text: That evening he approaches you again in the hotel lobby and asks about your organisation's plans for next year.

choices.label: I talk only about what is already public
choices.feedback: Correct. A pleasant chat can also be a way to collect information.

choices.label: I share details, it is not that secret
choices.feedback: Small details add up to a big picture. Keep non-public matters to yourself.

nodes.text: You are going out to dinner. Where does the laptop stay?

choices.label: I take it with me, or switch it off and lock it in the safe
choices.feedback: Well done. A device that is off, encrypted and in your control is best protected.

choices.label: On the desk, the screen is locked
choices.feedback: A screen lock helps, but anyone entering the room can tamper with the device.

points: Travel with minimum data, get the device checked on return.
VPN on unknown networks, your own charger in public.
Never leave devices unattended or plug in strangers' drives.
